lead: Data must travel from a source to a destination. Two fundamental ways to move that data are circuit switching, which reserves a dedicated path for the whole session, and packet switching, which lets many users share the same links by breaking data into packets. Circuit switching is used in traditional telephone networks, while packet switching underlies the Internet. Understanding the trade‑offs helps you choose the right technology for a given service.
prereq: You need: the basics of data communication from Data communication: components and data flow modes and the layered view from Protocols, standards and layered architecture.

blocks.text: In circuit switching a complete path from the source to the destination is reserved before any bits travel. The path stays reserved for the whole call, even if no data are sent at a particular moment. Because the bandwidth on each link is fixed, the user gets a guaranteed data rate. The propagation delay is constant for a given physical path, independent of bandwidth.

blocks.where: B is total bits transmitted (bits); R is reserved data rate (bits ⁄ s); T is call duration (s).

items: Determine the required data rate for the service (e.g., 64 kbps for a voice call).
Reserve a physical or logical path that can sustain that rate on every link.
Keep the path occupied for the entire session, regardless of actual traffic.
Predictable latency – useful for real‑time voice or video.
Inefficient use of bandwidth when the user is silent.
Simple switching hardware – the network only needs to connect two ends.

blocks.text: Packet switching breaks a message into small packets. Each packet carries a destination address and is forwarded independently. Links are shared among many users; If the outgoing link selected by the routing decision is free, the packet can be transmitted immediately; otherwise it is queued until the link becomes available.

blocks.where: D is total packet delay (s); L is packet length (bits); R is link data rate (bits ⁄ s); d_prop is propagation delay (seconds); Q is queuing delay (s) caused when total demand exceeds R.

items: Segment the data stream into packets of size L.
At each router, examine the packet header and forward to the next hop.
If the outgoing link is busy, place the packet in a queue; Q grows with traffic load.
Higher link utilization – idle periods of one user can be used by another.
Variable delay – queuing can increase latency during congestion.
More complex routing logic – packets may follow different paths.

sections.h3: When to prefer one over the other

blocks.text: Circuit switching is chosen when a constant data rate and low jitter are mandatory, such as a traditional land‑line call or a dedicated video‑conference link in a corporate campus. Packet switching is preferred for bursty traffic, web browsing, or any service that can tolerate some delay, because it makes better use of expensive bandwidth.

examples.question: A telephone network provides a dedicated 64 kbps circuit for a voice call lasting 10 minutes. Compute the total number of bits that can be transmitted on this circuit. In an IP network the same 64 kbps link is shared by 5 users, each generating traffic at an average rate of 20 kbps. If each user transmits continuously for 2 minutes, (a) how many bits does each user generate, (b) what is the total traffic generated, (c) how many bits can the link actually carry in 2 minutes, and (d) how many bits remain queued at the end of the 2‑minute interval.
steps: Circuit: B = R × T = 64 000 bits ⁄ s × 600 s = 38 400 000 bits = 38.4 Mbits.
Each packet‑switch user: B_user = 20 000 bits ⁄ s × 120 s = 2 400 000 bits = 2.4 Mbits.
Link capacity in 2 minutes: B_link = 64 000 bits ⁄ s × 120 s = 7 680 000 bits = 7.68 Mbits.
Queued bits = B_total – B_link = 12.0 Mbits – 7.68 Mbits = 4.32 Mbits.
examples.answer: The circuit can carry 38.4 Mbits. Each user generates 2.4 Mbits, total 12.0 Mbits, the link can transmit 7.68 Mbits in 2 minutes, leaving 4.32 Mbits queued.
examples.check:
R_circuit = 64000
T_call = 600
bits_circuit = R_circuit * T_call
R_user = 20000
T_user = 120
bits_user = R_user * T_user
bits_total = bits_user * 5
bits_link = R_circuit * T_user
bits_queue = bits_total - bits_link
print(bits_circuit/1e6)
print(bits_user/1e6)
print(bits_total/1e6)
print(bits_link/1e6)
print(bits_queue/1e6)
examples.output: Link can carry 7.68 Mbits in 2 minutes

traps: Assuming packet switching is always faster because it has no set‑up time; in reality queuing can add large delays.
Mixing up data rate (kbps) with total data transferred (Mbits) and forgetting to multiply by time.
Treating the 64 kbps link as able to carry 5 × 20 kbps simultaneously without checking the capacity limit.

quiz.q: What is the main resource that circuit switching reserves for a session?
quiz.a: A dedicated path (or set of channels) that provides a fixed bandwidth for the entire session.

quiz.q: Explain why packet switching can achieve higher link utilization than circuit switching.
quiz.a: Because packets from many users share the same link, idle periods of one user are used by others, reducing wasted bandwidth.

quiz.q: A video conference needs a constant 2 Mbps. If a circuit is set up with 2.5 Mbps capacity, how many bits can be sent in a 30‑minute call?
quiz.a: Use B = R × T: B = 2 500 000 bits ⁄ s × 1800 s = 4.5 × 10⁹ bits = 4.5 Gbits.

quiz.q: In a packet‑switched network a link of 10 Mbps carries packets of 1 000 bits. What is the transmission time for one packet (ignore queuing)?
quiz.a: Transmission time = L ⁄ R = 1 000 bits ÷ 10 000 000 bits ⁄ s = 0.0001 s = 100 µs.

quiz.q: Two users share a 5 Mbps link. User A sends at 3 Mbps continuously, User B at 4 Mbps intermittently. Sketch how the queuing delay for User B changes over time.
quiz.a: When User B is active, total demand = 7 Mbps > 5 Mbps, so a queue builds; when User B stops, the queue drains at 5 Mbps, reducing delay to zero.

quiz.q: Name one real‑world system that uses circuit switching.
Why does packet switching introduce variable latency?
quiz.a: Because each packet may experience different queuing times depending on the current traffic load on each link.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern telecoms use hybrid approaches: voice over IP runs on packet switching, while 5G core networks reserve slices that behave like circuits for ultra‑reliable low‑latency services. Research explores programmable data planes that can dynamically allocate circuit‑like resources on packet‑switched fabrics. Look for "network slicing" and "software‑defined networking" to see the next evolution.
